slides.kicker: NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 · Team Kosmic
slides.title: ORBI
slides.subtitle: From drift to decision.
text: A health autonomy console for astronauts on long-duration missions. Wearables pre-fill the vitals. In 90 seconds the astronaut confirms them, and a deterministic engine turns the day into an explained decision.
slides.footer: orbi.agustinpane.xyz · synthetic demo data · mission day 148
notes: Open with the person, not the product. On the way to Mars there is no clinic, no evacuation and up to 20 minutes of delay each way. The crew has to decide on board.
ORBI does not diagnose. It turns the daily check-in into a prioritized, explained and auditable decision.
Key line: from drift to decision.

slides.title: Day 148. Fourteen minutes from Earth, each way.
text: The commander slept 4.5 hours for the fifth night in a row. Her temperature is 37.9 °C. On Mars, nobody can examine her in real time, and the answer to a question leaves Earth after the clinical window has already moved.
Crews are trained, but they are not flight surgeons. Today the tools are a checklist and a delayed call.
notes: Make the room feel the distance. Fourteen minutes is the demo value; NASA talks about up to 20 minutes one way on Mars.
The clinical point: a conversation is not a decision loop. By the time Earth replies, the crew has already acted or lost time.
The second number is the physical cost of weightlessness: 1 to 1.5 percent of bone mineral density per month.

slides.title: Communication delay is a clinical variable.
text: The same CONCERN cannot be handled the same way at zero seconds and at fourteen minutes. ORBI makes latency part of the triage, not a network detail.

cards.label: ISS
cards.title: ≈ 0 s
cards.text: Flight surgeon now. Ground and crew share the same window.

cards.label: Moon
cards.title: ≈ 1.3 s
cards.text: Flight surgeon now, with a short round trip.

cards.label: Mars
cards.title: 14 min
cards.text: Local protocol first. The flight surgeon packet leaves on the next window.

callout.text: The farther you are, the more the decision has to live on board.

notes: This slide is the differentiator. Most health dashboards stop at a color. ORBI changes the escalation path with the mission.
On the ISS you call the flight surgeon. On Mars you act first and explain later. The crew is not replacing the doctor; it is buying the doctor time.
Say it plainly: latency is a clinical variable.

slides.title: A 90-second check-in that ends in a decision.
text: The watch and the biometric shirt already bring sleep, heart rate, SpO₂ and temperature. The astronaut confirms them and adds mood, fatigue and glucose.
No typing what the sensors already know. The check-in is the smallest possible input for a useful output.
bullets: Seven daily fields, one closed list: sleep, mood, fatigue, resting heart rate, temperature, SpO₂ and blood glucose.
The baseline is learned during 90 days of ground training (“train like you fly”); an opt-in cycle field keeps a luteal-phase rise from looking like an infection.
Every field answers “why we ask” in the UI, because the astronaut is not assumed to be a clinician.
The output is not a score. It is a level, a reason, an action and a person to notify.
notes: Walk the flow left to right. The wearables remove friction; the astronaut confirms; the engine decides; the UI explains; the escalation adapts.
The 90 seconds matter because adherence is the product. If the check-in is long, it will not happen on day 148.
The ground-training baseline is the “train like you fly” argument: ORBI learns what normal looks like before launch, not after the first anomaly.
Every field has a reason. That is also how we cover the brief's “do not assume the astronaut knows”.

slides.title: Six systems and a halo.
text: Every element on this body maps to one of NASA's five hazards of human spaceflight. That is why the map exists: it is an argument, not decoration.

cards.label: Gravity fields
cards.title: Cardiovascular
cards.text: Resting heart rate and blood pressure. The heart deconditions in microgravity.

cards.label: Gravity fields
cards.title: Musculoskeletal
cards.text: Estimated bone loss and exercise adherence. Bone density itself is Earth-only.

cards.label: Transversal
cards.title: Immune
cards.text: Temperature is the earliest signal a crew member can measure on board.

cards.label: Transversal
cards.title: Metabolic
cards.text: Glucose balance reflects nutrition, workload and metabolic risk.

cards.label: Hostile closed environment
cards.title: Respiratory
cards.text: SpO₂ separates a body problem from a cabin-air problem.

cards.label: Isolation and confinement
cards.title: Behavioral
cards.text: Sleep, mood and fatigue. The first signal is drift, not a crisis.

cards.label: Space radiation
cards.title: Radiation halo
cards.text: Cumulative dose against a mission budget, because deep-space limits are still open.

callout.text: Six systems and a halo. Each one has a NASA hazard behind it.

notes: This is the visual anchor of the pitch. Six systems, plus the radiation halo.
Map each one to the NASA Human Research Program hazards: gravity fields, hostile closed environment, isolation and confinement, space radiation, and distance from Earth as the escalation layer.
The body is clickable in the product: state, 30-day sparkline, baseline band and a short explanation of why the system matters.

slides.title: Explained triage, not a black box.
text: When a pattern appears, ORBI shows the level, the rule that fired, the evidence in numbers and the next action. The decision is the same today, tomorrow and in an audit.

columns.title: Because…
bullets: Sleep 4.5 h for five nights, below baseline
Resting heart rate 11 bpm above baseline

columns.title: Do this now
steps: Rest in crew quarters; mask in common areas

callout.text: Mars · CONCERN · local protocol first. The flight surgeon packet is queued for the next window.

notes: The judges will look for the “why”. Show that every alert carries its evidence, its threshold and its action.
Then switch the mission from Mars to ISS and show the escalation change without reloading. That is the moment the latency thesis lands.
Close with the product sentence: ORBI does not diagnose. It prioritizes, explains and escalates.

slides.title: One signal is noise. A pattern is a decision.
text: Four correlations carry the MVP. They are the difference between a dashboard and a decision-support tool.

rows: Early infection
Sleep < 6 h × 3 nights + temperature ≥ 37.5 °C + rising heart rate
Possible early infection, favored by sleep debt. Prepare the surgeon packet.
CONCERN
Cycle-aware
Temperature and resting heart rate up, but within her luteal-phase range; sleep normal; absolute thresholds not exceeded
Expected cycle variation, not infection. No action today.
NOMINAL
Cabin air
SpO₂ down and cabin CO₂ up in the same period
Cabin issue, not you. Fix ventilation; do not treat the patient.
WATCH + cabin alert
Solar event
An SPE is active
Go to shelter, run the checklist, log the dose, postpone the EVA.
URGENT

notes: The cabin-air row is the crowd favorite. The same SpO₂ drop can be the person or the room, and the answer changes the action.
The early-infection row is the main demo: sleep debt plus temperature plus heart rate. It is a correlation, not a single number.
The cycle-aware row is the second “not you” moment: a luteal-phase rise is expected, but a real fever still crosses the absolute threshold. The adjustment never relaxes clinical limits.
The solar event is the only URGENT in the demo. It changes the whole screen, not just a badge.

slides.title: Where we cannot measure, we say so.
text: Two things cannot be measured or fixed precisely in flight. ORBI does not invent a number to cover the gap.

cards.label: Estimated · NASA HRP
cards.title: Bone loss
cards.text: DXA only happens on Earth. ORBI estimates 1–1.5% per month and tracks the countermeasure that can be measured: exercise adherence.

cards.label: Budget · configurable
cards.title: Radiation
cards.text: NASA says deep-space exposure limits are still open. ORBI tracks the cumulative dose against a mission budget set by the medical team, with the 600 mSv career limit as a reference.

cards.label: Auditable
cards.title: Thresholds
cards.text: Every threshold lives in one file with a source and a verified flag. Unverified values stay visible instead of pretending to be settled.

callout.text: Where we cannot measure, we say so. That is how the rest stays trustworthy.

notes: This is an honesty slide, and it is a strength. Do not hide the gaps; name them before the judges do.
Bone density is measured with DXA on Earth. In flight we estimate from NASA HRP evidence and monitor exercise adherence.
Radiation: NASA itself says deep-space limits are unresolved. We show a budget and a trend, not a fake threshold.
The verified flag is not decoration. It tells a clinician which numbers are ready and which still need a primary source.

slides.title: Deterministic decisions. Optional explanations.
text: The engine is the product. The UI is a consumer of the engine, and an optional local model can explain the result but never compute it.
bullets: src/domain is pure TypeScript: no React, no DOM, no browser APIs.
The UI calls evaluate() and askCoach(). It never reimplements a clinical rule.
The template coach is the default and the fallback. A local LLM is an explanation layer validated by guardrails.
Guardrails reject diagnosis, medication, invented numbers and untriggered actions. If validation fails, the app falls back to the template.
Static SPA. No backend, no database, no decision ML, no computer vision.

callout.text: The decision is auditable. The explanation is optional.

notes: This is where a technical judge leans in. The domain is pure TypeScript, and the decision engine is deterministic.
We did not add ML to the decision path. In space medicine, explainability beats a marginal accuracy gain when the output drives an action.
The optional local model only rewrites the explanation from structured facts. The guardrails and the template fallback keep the app safe when the model fails.

slides.title: Official sources, with the gaps left visible.

rows: NASA HRP — Five Hazards of Human Spaceflight
Body map, sleep and circadian context, latency up to 20 minutes, 1–1.5% bone loss per month
NASA HRP — Evidence Report: Bone Fracture
Bone rules, exercise as the countermeasure, risk after returning from Mars
NASA-STD-3001
Cabin CO₂ and the 600 mSv career limit; the limit is confirmed by the women's health review (single value since 2022)
External reviews — women's health and ground training
Cycle-aware baseline (opt-in and private), 90-day ground-training baseline and 600 mSv as a single 2022 limit
CSA — Monitoring radiation for astronaut health
Continuous, autonomous radiation tracking and the halo concept
Clinical standards and ADA
Temperature, SpO₂, resting heart rate and glucose ranges

callout.text: We cite NASA and CSA in the app and in the submission. The unverified numbers are labeled as unverified.

notes: We read the official resources before writing the rules. The summaries live in docs/recursos.
Only the bone evidence gives directly applicable numbers. Most other thresholds are standard clinical ranges or NASA-STD-3001 references, and they are flagged for verification.
That is deliberate. A clinician should be able to audit the rules file without reading the UI.

slides.title: What you can open today.
text: The deterministic engine, the four current scenarios, the coach guardrails and the deployment are live. The Level 0 screens and the cycle-aware engine are landing on top of the same contract.
steps: Open the engine console and pick early-infection.
Set the mission to Mars, then to ISS: the escalation changes.
Switch to cabin-co2: the app says cabin issue, not you.
Switch to solar-event: the radiation halo goes urgent.

callout.text: 90 seconds of check-in. One explained decision.

notes: Keep the demo short and rehearsed. The console is the honest, working surface today.
The three scenario switches are the story: infection, environment and radiation.
The cycle-aware baseline and the luteal-phase scenario are the next engine step; do not present them as live until P3 is deployed.
Do not claim that the Today/Body/Decision screens are finished if they are not. Say they are landing on the same engine contract.
